name: Jamal Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing business management. A normal week is three lectures, a marketing seminar and a lot of time in the library, though I mostly study in my flat on Canal Row. On Sundays I go to church with my family, and on Saturday mornings I help in the family bakery, which has three shops. My parents pay for everything, so I don't have a part-time job, and I'm a bit embarrassed by that.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Because I'm going to run the bakeries one day, and Dad said I should learn the books and people side properly. My results were average, so I was lucky to get in. I don't use AI tools at all. Some of my classmates do, and I think it's like having someone else do your press-ups.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected. The big companies oversold it. I'd tell people at church and at the bakery that good work and honest customers matter more than machines. My dad would say the same, loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I can follow my plan: finish the degree, work in the bakeries, learn every job from the ovens to the accounts, and take over in about ten years. The pressure is the usual, like flour prices, rent and competition from supermarkets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working Saturdays at the bakery and ask to take over one task each term, like ordering or rotas. I'd keep up the degree with decent marks. And I'd save part of my allowance so I can put my own money into the family business someday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's like how things have always been, which suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you in the plateau, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarkets selling cheaper bread, and my dad getting older. He works six days a week and won't slow down. I worry he'll get ill and I won't be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would being ready look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing the suppliers, the staff and the numbers. At the moment Dad holds it all in his head, and that's a risk.

My dad would say the same, **loudly**.
think: I can follow my plan: finish the degree, work in the **bakeries**, and take over in about ten years.
The usual pressures remain: flour **prices**, rent and supermarkets.
do: Keep working **Saturdays** at the bakery and take over ordering or rotas.
Keep the degree up with decent **marks**.
Save part of my **allowance** to invest in the family business.
feel: **Calm**, because it's like how things have always been.
S0.quote: At the moment Dad holds it all in his head, and that's a risk.
fieldNote: **Traditional** and resistant; the bakery gives him a clear path.
Real worry is his father's **health** and the family business's key-person risk.
Sees AI use among classmates as **cheating**, not a skill.

steps.text: Work Saturdays at the bakery and take over the ordering
Save part of my allowance for the family business
Learn the suppliers, staff and numbers from Dad

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's more fuss than it's worth. A lot of office jobs will change, but people still need bread, and people still want to deal with a person. I'd say to my classmates that they should learn a trade or a real business, not only how to type at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not too worried. My degree is a nice-to-have, since I'll be in the bakery. If AI does the paperwork and ordering, fine, though I'd want to see it work first. Some classmates are going to struggle to find desk jobs, and I feel for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working in the bakery and learn the ovens and the ordering. If the ordering software gets easier, I'd let my brother Marc try it first, since he likes that stuff. I'd keep studying, because Dad insists on it. I'd also learn about the staff, since people stay when they're treated well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. This one changes the world around me, but not my place in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the classmates you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them there's nothing wrong with learning a trade. People look down on a trade, but a baker who runs three shops makes a decent living. And I'd offer to help, if anyone wanted a job in the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use AI in the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for things like predicting orders, if it's cheap and tested. But I'd want to see another baker use it for a year first. I don't want to be the guinea pig.

fieldNote: Sees hands-on **work** as a safe place and shows some pride in it.
Waits for **proof** and lets his brother try new tools first.

steps.text: Learn the ovens, ordering and staff rotas at the bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should keep calm and look after our own. I'd say families and churches will have to step up, because governments won't be ready in two years. And I'd say that business owners should keep their staff as long as they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious. The bakery is hands-on until 2031, but the thinking side, like orders, accounts and marketing, would change at once. My degree would be worth less, and the supermarkets with their big tech would undercut us. People might also spend less if they lose their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dad we should cut costs now and build a cash reserve. I'd drop non-essential things and focus on learning the oven side, not just management. I'd ask our priest and the neighbours about starting a local food-sharing scheme, so we're ready to help others. And I'd keep studying, though more slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried and a bit sick. I'd pray more, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'll look after them as long as we can, and that I'd rather cut my own pay than let anyone go. I don't know if I could keep that promise, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the two-year warning change how you act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I wouldn't wait. If I had ten years I'd move slowly, but with two I'd tighten up right now, before anyone else does.

I'd say families and **churches** will have to step up.
think: The bakery is hands-on until 2031, but the **thinking** side would change at once.
People might **spend** less if they lose their jobs.

fieldNote: Anxiety comes from **customers** losing income, not his own job.
Turns to **church** and community before government.
Says he would **cut** his own pay to protect staff, a clear value.

steps.text: Tell Dad to cut costs and hold a cash reserve
Ask our priest about a local food-sharing scheme
Spend more shifts learning the ovens and production

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready, and people should start. I'd tell friends that family businesses and trades have the most steady ground. I'd say the government should leave businesses alone to adapt, and not make it harder with new rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy but not scared. By 2031 I'd be 23, probably running one shop, and the machines could do the accounts and orders. The ovens would still need people until about 2034. I'd worry about the supermarkets using robots sooner than us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take on one shop's management, and slowly bring in tools that have proven themselves. I'd keep savings as a buffer. I'd also train a few of our young staff to do more than one job, because flexible people are what a family business needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. The family business is a good anchor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the supermarkets?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compete on quality and relationships. We know our customers by name, and supermarket machines won't do that. But I'd watch the prices closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept help from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it's temporary and tied to work, like a training grant for staff. I'm not keen on handouts, but I'd take help if it's a fair deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and there's no reason for panic. I'd tell friends to work hard, save, and look after their families. Things always change, and honest work always finds a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel fine. By 2036 I'd be 28, with a family perhaps, and the bakery would be mine. Machines might do a lot of the thinking, but the bread and the people won't change much. I'd worry more for the people who work in offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work every job in the bakery, and take over gradually. I'd try new tools only when they've been proven by other bakers. And I'd put some money aside every month, because I'd like to buy a fourth shop by around 2036 if things go well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like the same life as now, just a bit bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about a family of your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope to marry in a few years. My wife and I would live above one of the shops, like my grandparents did. Church, children and a shop: that's the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would AI change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the paperwork. The rest depends on people, and I don't see that changing.

I'd tell friends to work hard, save, and look after their **families**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28 and the **bakery** would be mine.
The bread and the people won't change much, but I'd worry for **office** workers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is too fast, and the supermarkets and customers could change faster than a family bakery can. What would help is clear warning from government, and help for small businesses to keep staff, but I wouldn't want a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No. I just want to say I'm lucky and I know it. My family's work is real and in front of me, and some people in my classes have nothing like that.

headlineQuote: My family's work is real and in front of me, and some people in my classes have nothing like that.
portrait: Jamal is an 18-year-old **business** management student from a family that owns three bakeries and pays his fees and rent.
He never uses AI tools, wants proof before changing anything, and plans to take over the **bakeries** in about ten years.
He is traditional: church, family and honest work come first, and he prefers **temporary**, work-linked help over handouts.
He stays calm in most worlds, but becomes **anxious** at two years, when customers' spending could drop.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world worries him most, because supermarkets and customers could change faster than a family bakery can.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **warning** from government and work-linked help for small businesses to keep their staff, not a handout.
